article.titel: I Wasted Another Year: A Fair Review and One Next Step
article.h1: I Wasted Another Year: What Can I Do Now?
article.desc: Feel like you wasted another year? Use a practical review to separate regret from facts, choose one unfinished priority, and decide your next small action.
article.antwoord: If you feel like you wasted another year, start by naming what actually went unfinished. Then look at what your time required, what you maintained, and what you still want. Use that evidence to choose one next action. You do not have to declare the year a success or rebuild your whole life tonight.

secties.kop: Name the disappointment instead of judging your whole life
alineas: Perhaps you planned to change jobs, learn something, reconnect with a friend, or finish a project. December is approaching and that change has not happened. It makes sense to feel disappointed. But a specific disappointment and the conclusion that your entire life is wasted are different statements.

Write the unfinished thing as a sentence someone else could understand. Replace 'I achieved nothing' with 'I wanted to finish my portfolio, and I have two pages left.' If you cannot make it specific, list the two or three things that are bothering you most. You are looking for something you can examine, not a verdict on your worth.

This guide is a reflection exercise for disappointment about unfinished goals. It is not a diagnosis or a substitute for support when distress is persistent or makes daily life difficult. If that describes your situation, consider talking with someone you trust or a qualified professional rather than trying to solve everything with another productivity plan.

secties.kop: Make a fair record of the year
alineas: Look through your calendar, notes, and completed tasks. Do not rely only on how this week feels. On a sheet of paper, make three columns: wanted, happened, and context. The first holds your original intention. The second holds observable events. The third holds responsibilities or limits that affected the plan.

For example: wanted, finish a course; happened, completed three modules; context, worked additional shifts for two months. That does not magically finish the course. It gives you a more useful starting point than calling yourself lazy. Include maintenance work, such as caring for someone, keeping a household running, or meeting existing commitments, when it was part of your actual year.

You do not need to turn every hard experience into a lesson. Some events were simply painful, unfair, or outside your control. A fair review leaves room for both loss and progress. It also distinguishes 'I chose something else' from 'I could not do everything at once.'
lijst: Wanted: What change did I expect to see?
Happened: What would my calendar or work show?
Context: What took time or limited my choices?

alineas: An unfinished goal is not automatically a goal you should carry forward. Ask whether you still want the outcome, whether the original plan was realistic, and whether pursuing it would crowd out something more important. You may choose to continue, resize, or close it.

Imagine a hobby project you started because friends were excited about it. If it no longer matters to you, closing it may free attention for a commitment you actually value. By contrast, a course that still matters might need a smaller weekly commitment rather than a dramatic new deadline.

Choose only one unfinished priority for this exercise. The others can remain on a separate list without becoming promises for tomorrow. Name the smallest useful result you want next: one finished portfolio page, one appointment requested, or one lesson completed. Make it something observable.

secties.kop: Take responsibility without making self-criticism the plan
alineas: Being fair to yourself does not mean pretending your choices had no consequences. If you avoided a task, broke a commitment, or spent time in a way you regret, name the behavior and decide what to repair. Avoid turning that description into a permanent identity.

Breines and Chen's 2012 paper reports four experiments in which self-compassion after a weakness or mistake was associated with greater motivation to improve in the tested tasks. These findings do not establish that a kind sentence fixes long-term regret. They offer a reason to question the assumption that harsh self-judgment is necessary for effort.

Try writing two sentences: 'I wish I had done ___ differently.' Then: 'The action I can take responsibility for now is ___.' The second sentence should describe behavior, such as apologizing, asking for feedback, or opening the project, rather than an instruction to become a better person.

secties.kop: Give the next action a place and a check
alineas: Choose when and where you will attempt the action, and decide what counts as done. 'Work on my future' is hard to check. 'After lunch on Thursday, open the portfolio file and edit the introduction for ten minutes' has a clear beginning and a manageable scope.

Harkin and colleagues' meta-analysis of 138 studies found that interventions promoting progress monitoring improved goal attainment on average. That result is about groups and varied goals, not a prediction for your particular week. A simple written record is a practical way to make your own follow-through visible.

At the next check, record what happened. If you did the action, choose whether to repeat it. If you did not, examine the obstacle before making the plan more demanding. Was the time unavailable, the first step unclear, or the task no longer important? Adjust one thing and try again.

secties.kop: You can begin before the calendar changes
alineas: You do not need to wait for January to make one useful choice. Dai, Milkman, and Riis found increases in several aspirational behaviors following calendar landmarks in three field studies. Starting a new week or month can be a helpful cue, but the findings do not promise that a fresh date creates lasting change.

If a date gives you a useful boundary, use it. If waiting for that date postpones an action you could take now, choose a nearer moment. A new beginning can be modest: a scheduled conversation, a revised plan, or a task you finally stop carrying.

The review below is an original practical structure, not a tested treatment or a promise to recover a year. Copy it into a notebook. You can complete it without buying anything. If you later want a paper format for repeated habit check-ins, the Lasting Change Workbook paperback is an optional next step. The free seven-day reset guide is the next read when you are ready to turn this review into a first-week plan.
Use short, concrete answers. Leave a line blank if you do not know yet. A useful review gives you a clearer decision, not another list of everything you think you should become.
lijst: The unfinished goal I am disappointed about is: ___.
The evidence of what actually happened is: ___.
The responsibilities or constraints I need to acknowledge are: ___.
My decision is to continue, resize, or close this goal because: ___.
I will attempt it at ___, in ___.
At my next check on ___, I will record what happened and adjust one thing.

faq: What if I really did waste a lot of time?

You can acknowledge that without extending the judgment to your whole life. Pick one behavior you regret, identify what it displaced, and decide whether a repair or a smaller plan is possible. The aim is a useful next choice, not an argument that every hour was worthwhile.
Is it too late to change before the year ends?

It may be too late for a particular original deadline. That does not prevent you from finishing a smaller part, asking for help, or choosing a realistic next step. Avoid making a rushed life overhaul just to make a calendar year look better.
How is this different from starting over?

This review comes before a reset plan. It helps you decide what the unfinished year actually means and which goal still deserves your effort. The separate seven-day guide focuses on organizing the first week after you make that decision.
Do I need a workbook to do the review?
No. A plain sheet of paper or a note is enough. The optional paperback is for readers who want a structured format for ongoing habit check-ins, rather than a requirement for using this free exercise.
